cards.title: The NatWest and Ulster Bank batch failure
cards.sub: 17 June – 10 July 2012 · Technology Services, RBS Group
cards.prompt: An overnight batch scheduler stops putting jobs in its queues after an upgrade is backed out. On what date was it backed out, how many customers were affected, and what did the banks pay back in redress?
cards.body: Technology Services upgraded NatWest's and Ulster Bank's batch scheduler from Version 1 to Version 2A, a patched build, then on 19 June 2012 backed it out — having only ever tested backing out unpatched Version 2. Jobs stopped appearing in the queues. 6.5 million customers; £70.3 million in redress; a £42 million FCA fine.
cards.answer: Backed out 19 June 2012 (upgraded 17 June); at least 6.5 million customers; £70.3 million in redress, plus a £42 million FCA fine.

cards.title: One statement, both failures
cards.sub: 2012 · zero fires and two fires in the same accounts
cards.prompt: RBS's recovery was staff re-loading jobs into the batch queues by hand. Why could they not simply replay the batch, and what did customers then find on a single statement?
cards.body: Order is the semantics — out of sequence gives wrong balances and interest — so there was no replay button, only manual re-loading. Customers found standing orders that never ran and "duplicated entries on their statements": zero fires and two fires in the same accounts, because a re-loaded job carried no key to dedupe against.
cards.answer: Sequence determines balances and interest, so replay was not safe — recovery was manual. Customers got standing orders that never ran and duplicated entries on the same statements: the missing fire and the double fire together, with no idempotency key to stop the second.

cards.title: FCA Final Notice, RBS/NatWest/Ulster Bank
cards.prompt: Which document gives the day-by-day account of the failure, and how does it define what a batch scheduler is actually for?
cards.body: The FCA's Final Notice of 19 November 2014. Paragraph 4.5: "Batch schedulers place the jobs into queues and ensure that each job is processed in the correct sequence. That day's batch processing is complete when all balances are final." Its Annex records that the FCA and the PRA agreed in April 2013 to investigate the incident jointly.
cards.answer: The FCA Final Notice of 19 November 2014, product of a joint FCA/PRA investigation. Para 4.5: schedulers queue jobs and process them in the correct sequence; the batch is done when all balances are final.

cards.title: Tracey McDermott
cards.sub: 2014 · FCA director of enforcement and financial crime
cards.prompt: Who announced the fine, what did she say modern banking depends on, and what was procedurally unprecedented about the action?
cards.body: Tracey McDermott, FCA director of enforcement and financial crime: "Modern banking depends on effective, reliable and resilient IT systems." It was the first joint enforcement action by the FCA and the PRA. Her case was not mis-selling or bad lending — it was an untested rollback of a batch scheduler.
cards.answer: Tracey McDermott, FCA director of enforcement and financial crime. "Modern banking depends on effective, reliable and resilient IT systems." First-ever joint FCA/PRA enforcement action.
